extra.message: Missing Authentication on All CRUD Endpoints — Any anonymous attacker can read, create, modify, and delete any user record in the system with no credentials or identity verification. [verified: The FastAPI app (line 42-51) is created with no authentication middleware, no dependency injection for auth, and no session management; all CRUD endpoints are publicly accessible to any anonymous client with no credentials required.]

SQL Injection in GET /select — Full database compromise — attacker can read all user records including password hashes, modify data, or drop tables. [verified: User-controlled `username` query parameter from GET /select is interpolated directly into a SQL f-string (`f'SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = "{username}";'`) at line 184 with no parameterization, escaping, or input validation, and executed via aiosqlite in `run_sql_query`.]

NoSQL Injection in POST /find — Full NoSQL database compromise — attacker can bypass query filters, enumerate all records, execute arbitrary JavaScript via $where, and cause denial of service. [verified: The entire request body JSON from POST /find is passed directly to MontyDB's `users.find(query)` at line 227 with zero filtering, allowing injection of MongoDB operators ($where, $regex, etc.) and arbitrary JavaScript execution.]

SQL Injection in DELETE /user via username parameter — Arbitrary data deletion — attacker can delete any or all user records from the SQL database. [verified: User-controlled `username` query parameter in DELETE /user is interpolated directly into `f'DELETE FROM users WHERE username = "{username}";'` at line 233 with no sanitization or parameterization.]

Password Hash Exposure in Multi-Record SQL Query Responses — An attacker can retrieve all users' password hashes from the API response by triggering multi-row queries via SQL injection. [verified: `run_sql_query` at line 164 returns `{'users': _data}` for multi-row results including the raw password hash at tuple index 3; only the single-row path (lines 155-162) explicitly excludes index 3, so SQL-injection-induced multi-row queries leak all hashes.]

Weak Password Hashing with Unsalted MD5 — Stored password hashes can be cracked via rainbow tables or brute-force; identical passwords produce identical hashes enabling traffic analysis. If the database is ever exposed, all user passwords are trivially recoverable. [verified: Password hashing at line 191 uses `md5(user.password.encode()).hexdigest()` with no salt, making stored hashes vulnerable to rainbow-table and brute-force attacks; identical passwords produce identical hashes.]

Unauthenticated Database Reset via POST /reset — Complete data loss — attacker can repeatedly wipe the entire database, destroying all user records and causing denial of service. [verified: POST /reset at line 246 deletes both SQLite and NoSQL database files and reinitializes them with no authentication, authorization, rate limiting, or confirmation mechanism of any kind.]

Missing Rate Limiting on All Endpoints — Attackers can brute-force operations, enumerate users, cause resource exhaustion, and conduct denial-of-service attacks without any throttling. [verified: No rate-limiting middleware (slowapi, fastapi-limiter, or custom) is applied to any endpoint; all routes including destructive ones (POST /reset, DELETE /user) accept unlimited requests.]

User Enumeration via GET /select Response Differentiation — An unauthenticated attacker can enumerate valid usernames in the system by observing whether the response is an object (user exists) or {"users": []} (user does not exist), facilitating targeted credential attacks. [verified: GET /select returns a single-user dict ({id, name, username,...}) when found vs {'users': []} when not found (run_sql_query lines 154-167), with no authentication, authorization, or rate-limiting on the endpoint—classic structural response differentiation enabling username enumeration.]

Denial of Service via Unbounded Request Body in PUT /user — An attacker can exhaust server memory and disk by sending extremely large string values in the PUT /user JSON body, degrading or crashing the API service and filling the database with junk data. [verified: PUT /user accepts a Pydantic User model where all six fields are bare str with no max_length/min_length/regex constraints (lines 25-31); no ASGI middleware, body-size limit, or rate-limiting exists anywhere in the application, allowing an attacker to send multi-gigabyte strings that are interpolated into an f-string INSERT and stored, consuming server memory and database space.]

User Enumeration via GET /find Response Differentiation — An unauthenticated attacker can enumerate valid usernames through the NoSQL endpoint by observing whether the response is a user object vs [], enabling targeted attacks against known accounts. [verified: GET /find returns a user dict when found vs an empty tuple serialized as [] when not found (get_nosql_users lines 172-174), with no auth gate, providing the same enumeration vector through the NoSQL code path.]

API Documentation Exposure Bypassing docs_url=False — Full API schema disclosure — attackers gain a complete map of all endpoints, request formats, and data models, significantly aiding targeted exploitation. [verified: Despite `docs_url=False` and `redoc_url=False` (line 50-51), manual `/docs` (line 268) and `/redoc` (line 272) endpoints serve full Swagger UI, and the default `/openapi.json` endpoint remains active, exposing the complete API schema to anonymous clients.]

Missing Security Headers and Permissive CORS Configuration — The API is vulnerable to cross-origin attacks; lack of security headers weakens browser-side defenses and exposes the API to clickjacking, MIME-sniffing, and other client-side attacks. [verified: No CORSMiddleware is added and no security headers (Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, CSP) are configured; in a pure API context the practical risk is lower but cross-origin attacks remain possible if consumed by browsers.]
